lessons.title: Sharpening Principles and Angles
lessons.body: Every cutting tool works best when its edge is sharp and at the correct angle. The angle is the angle between the two faces of the blade at the cutting edge. For most agricultural tools, the bevel angle (the angle of the ground edge) is what you control. A smaller angle cuts easier but is weaker; a larger angle is stronger but cuts slower. For machetes and slashers, use a 20â25 degree bevel. For hoes and axes, 25â30 degrees. For pruning shears and knives, 15â20 degrees. You can measure angles with a simple protractor or by using a preâset sharpening guide. In the field, you can estimate: a matchbook cover is about 15 degrees, a coin about 30 degrees. Always sharpen on the bevel side only, unless the tool is designed to be sharpened on both sides (like a knife). Maintain a consistent angle with each stroke. If you rock the blade, you round the edge. Check sharpness by slicing paper or shaving arm hair. A dull edge bruises plants and makes you work harder. A sharp edge saves time and energy.

lessons.title: Using Bench Grinders and Belt Sanders
lessons.body: A bench grinder is a fast way to remove metal and set a new bevel on a damaged edge. Use a 6â or 8âinch grinder with a 60âgrit wheel for rough shaping and a 120âgrit wheel for finer work. Always wear safety glasses and a dust mask. Hold the blade at the desired angle (20â25 degrees for machetes) and press lightly against the wheel. Move the blade side to side to avoid overheating. Overheating turns the steel blue and softens it. If you see blue, dip the blade in water immediately. A belt sander with a 2x72âinch belt is more forgiving. Use 80âgrit for shaping, 120âgrit for sharpening, and 400âgrit for polishing. Run the belt at moderate speed and keep the blade moving. For a machete, grind from the base to the tip in smooth strokes. After grinding, remove the burr (a thin wire edge) by honing. In Africa, many workshops use a simple waterâcooled grindstone or a treadleâpowered grinder. If you use a dry grinder, cool the blade often in a bucket of water. Never grind a blade that is too hot to touch. A belt sander can also be used to sharpen hoes and axes, but be careful not to round the tip. Practice on a scrap piece of mild steel before working on a good tool.

lessons.title: Sharpening with Whetstones and Files
lessons.body: Whetstones are the traditional way to sharpen tools. They come in natural or synthetic forms and in different grits. A combination stone with 250âgrit on one side and 1000âgrit on the other is ideal. Soak a waterstone in water for 10â15 minutes before use; oil stones use a few drops of honing oil. Place the stone on a stable surface. Hold the blade at the correct angle (20â25 degrees) and push it across the stone in a circular or diagonal motion. Use light pressure and keep the angle steady. Count 10â20 strokes on one side, then check for a burr on the opposite side. Once you feel a burr along the entire edge, flip the blade and do the same number of strokes on the other side to remove the burr. For a file, use a singleâcut mill file or a diamond file. Clamp the blade in a vise and push the file away from you at a 20âdegree angle. Files cut in one direction only; lift the file on the return stroke. For axes and hoes, a 10âinch mill file works well. In Africa, many farmers use a smooth river stone or a piece of broken grinding wheel. These can work if you keep them wet and maintain a consistent angle. After sharpening, clean the stone with water and a brush. Store it dry. A wellâmaintained stone will last for years.

lessons.title: Honing and Polishing Edges
lessons.body: Honing removes the burr and polishes the edge to make it razor sharp. After sharpening on a coarse stone or grinder, you need a finer abrasive. A leather strop charged with polishing compound (like jeweler's rouge or chromium oxide) is ideal. You can make a strop from an old belt glued to a board. Apply a little compound and rub it in. Draw the blade across the strop with the edge trailing (spine first) at a slightly higher angle than the sharpening angle (about 25â30 degrees). Use light pressure and do 10â20 strokes per side. For a polished edge, use a 4000â8000 grit waterstone. Soak it, then use light strokes, alternating sides. The goal is to refine the scratch pattern until it looks like a mirror. A polished edge cuts smoother and lasts longer. For pruning shears, a felt wheel on a drill with polishing compound works well. In the field, you can use a piece of cardboard or newspaper with a little toothpaste as a makeshift strop. After honing, clean the blade with alcohol or soapy water. Dry it and apply a thin coat of oil (coconut, mineral, or machine oil) to prevent rust. Test the edge by slicing a ripe tomato or shaving a thin slice of paper. If it catches, keep honing. A honed edge is safer because it requires less force to cut.

lessons.title: Repairing Damaged Edges
lessons.body: Damaged edges have chips, nicks, or cracks. You must remove the damage before sharpening. For a small nick, use a coarse diamond file or a 60âgrit belt to grind the edge back until the nick is gone. For a large chip, you may need to reshape the entire edge with a bench grinder. Work slowly and cool the blade often. If the tip is broken off a machete, you can reâprofile it by grinding a new curve from the spine down to the edge. Keep the original bevel angle. After grinding, the edge will be rough; progress to a 120âgrit belt, then a 250âgrit stone, then hone. For a bent blade, do not hammer it coldâit may crack. Heat it to a dull red (about 700Â°C) with a torch or forge, straighten it with a hammer and anvil, then let it cool slowly. This anneals the steel, so you must reâharden and temper it if it's a highâcarbon tool. For simple mild steel hoes, straightening cold is often fine. If a handle is loose, see Lesson 6. After repair, test the tool on a piece of wood. If it cuts without leaving marks, the repair is good. Always wear gloves and eye protection when grinding. In rural Africa, many tools are repaired by local blacksmiths who use charcoal forges. If you have access to one, they can reâforge a damaged edge quickly.

lessons.title: Maintaining Tool Handles and Fixings
lessons.body: A sharp edge is useless if the handle is loose or broken. Check handles regularly for cracks, splinters, and looseness. For wooden handles, sand smooth with 80â then 120âgrit sandpaper. Apply a coat of boiled linseed oil or used motor oil to protect against moisture and rot. Let it dry for 24 hours. If the handle is loose, remove the old wedge and reâhandle. For an axe or hoe, drive a new wooden wedge (hardwood like mukwa or mahogany) into the eye from the top. Then drive a metal wedge crosswise for extra security. For a machete, the handle is often held by rivets or a ferrule. Tighten rivets by hammering them gently on an anvil. If the ferrule is loose, replace it with a piece of copper pipe or a metal washer. For file handles, ensure the ferrule is tight and the handle is free of cracks. In Africa, many handles are made from local hardwoods like ebony, teak, or acacia. These are durable but need oiling. Avoid using fresh green wood; it shrinks and loosens. Store tools with the blade covered and the handle oiled. Hang tools rather than leaving them on the ground. Check fixings before each use: a loose head can fly off and cause injury. A wellâmaintained handle makes the tool safer and more efficient. Replace any handle that is cracked or splintered.

quiz.q: What is the recommended bevel angle for a machete?
quiz.explanation: A 20â25 degree bevel balances sharpness and durability for machetes.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for fast metal removal when reshaping a damaged edge?
quiz.explanation: A bench grinder with a coarse wheel removes metal quickly for reshaping.

quiz.q: What should you do if a blade turns blue while grinding?
options: B) Dip it in water immediately
quiz.explanation: Blue color indicates overheating that softens steel; cooling prevents damage.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a burr when sharpening?
options: A) It indicates the edge is sharp
B) It makes the blade dull
D) It is a type of handle
quiz.explanation: A burr forms when the two bevels meet, showing the edge is thin and sharp.

quiz.q: Which grit waterstone is used for polishing an edge?
quiz.explanation: High grit stones (4000â8000) refine and polish the edge to a mirror finish.

quiz.q: How should you store a whetstone?
quiz.explanation: Whetstones should be dried and stored dry to prevent cracking or mold.

quiz.q: What is the correct motion when using a file to sharpen a blade?
quiz.explanation: Files cut in one direction; lift on the return stroke to avoid dulling.

quiz.q: Which of these is a makeshift strop material?
quiz.explanation: Cardboard or newspaper with toothpaste can polish an edge in the field.

quiz.q: What angle should you use when honing on a strop?
quiz.explanation: A slightly higher angle ensures the very edge is polished without rounding it.

quiz.q: What should you do before sharpening a chipped edge?
options: B) Remove the chip by grinding
quiz.explanation: The chip must be ground away to restore a continuous edge.

quiz.q: How can you straighten a bent highâcarbon blade?
options: B) Heat to dull red and straighten
quiz.explanation: Heating to dull red makes the steel malleable for straightening without cracking.

quiz.q: What is a common sign that a handle needs reâhandling?
quiz.explanation: A loose handle is dangerous and indicates the wedge or rivets need attention.

quiz.q: Which oil is recommended for protecting wooden handles?
quiz.explanation: Boiled linseed oil penetrates and protects wood from moisture and rot.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a metal wedge in an axe handle?
quiz.explanation: A metal wedge expands the wood to lock the head in place.

quiz.q: Which grit is used on a belt sander for initial shaping?
quiz.explanation: 80 grit removes material quickly for shaping a new bevel.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of overheating a blade during grinding?
options: B) It loses temper and softens
quiz.explanation: Overheating draws the temper, making the steel soft and unable to hold an edge.

quiz.q: How many strokes per side are typical when honing on a strop?
quiz.explanation: 10â20 light strokes per side are sufficient to remove the burr and polish.

quiz.q: Which of these is a natural sharpening stone found in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Smooth river stones are commonly used as makeshift whetstones in rural areas.

quiz.q: What should you do after sharpening to prevent rust?
options: B) Apply a thin coat of oil
C) Store in a damp place
quiz.explanation: A thin oil film protects the steel from moisture and rust.

quiz.q: What is the correct angle for sharpening pruning shears?
quiz.explanation: Pruning shears typically use a 15â20 degree bevel for clean cuts.

quiz.q: How can you test if a tool is sharp?
quiz.explanation: Slicing paper or shaving hair tests the edge's ability to cut cleanly.

quiz.q: What is a burr?
quiz.explanation: A burr is a thin ridge of metal that forms on the opposite side of the sharpened edge.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for removing a small nick from a blade?
quiz.explanation: A coarse diamond file quickly grinds away small nicks.

quiz.q: What is the first step when repairing a damaged edge?
quiz.explanation: The damaged portion must be ground away before sharpening can be effective.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good hardwood for tool handles in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Mukwa is a dense, durable hardwood commonly used for tool handles.

quiz.q: What should you do if a handle is cracked?
quiz.explanation: A cracked handle is unsafe and should be replaced.

quiz.q: How often should you check tool fixings?
quiz.explanation: Checking before use prevents accidents from loose heads or handles.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a ferrule on a tool handle?
quiz.explanation: A ferrule reinforces the handle where it meets the blade, preventing splitting.

quiz.q: Which grit belt would you use for final sharpening on a belt sander?
quiz.explanation: 400 grit refines the edge after coarser grits.

quiz.q: What is the recommended way to store tools?
quiz.explanation: Hanging prevents damage and covering the blade protects the edge and people.
